argument: Sartre rejects the popular 'hidden soul' model of the self as a stable inner personality accessible only to oneself, arguing instead that the self is constituted by the entangled interplay of facticity (the facts currently true about you, modeled on being-in-itself) and transcendence (your possibilities, modeled on being-for-itself) -- a freedom that is always 'freedom within limitations,' as the haiku analogy shows. Because confronting this duality produces anxiety, people flee into 'bad faith,' collapsing themselves into pure facticity or pure transcendence (illustrated by Sartre's café waiter), covertly seeking to 'become God.' Sartre adds a third category, being-for-others, showing the self is partly constituted by how others perceive us; ultimately, who you are is the conglomeration of everything you've actually done, not your private self-narrative, since (as the Napoleon delusion and Walmart hero examples show) others sometimes have superior epistemic access to your true character.
keyIdeas: Sartre rejects the popular/Christian-derived 'hidden soul' model, in which your 'true self' is a stable, private inner personality accessible only to you and intimates, distinct from a social 'mask.'

Facticity is the totality of objective facts currently true about a person, analogous to being-in-itself; transcendence is a person's capacity to change and the possibilities open to them, analogous to being-for-itself -- the two are mutually entangled, since facts constrain possibilities while choices generate new facts. Freedom is thus never absolute but 'freedom within limitations,' as the haiku analogy shows.

'Bad faith' is the tactic of fleeing the anxiety of facticity/transcendence duality by collapsing entirely into one side or the other -- pretending to be pure facticity (a fixed role) or pure transcendence (unlimited possibility), as Sartre's café waiter illustrates by reducing himself to pure 'waiterliness.'

The covert desire behind bad faith is to 'become God': the traditional God is imagined as both perfect/complete (pure facticity) and omnipotent (pure transcendence), and bad faith covertly seeks both at once.

'Being-for-others,' Sartre's third ontological category, holds that the self is partly constituted by how others perceive and judge us; who you really are is 'the conglomeration of all the things you've ever actually done,' not your private self-narrative, and (as the Napoleon delusion and Walmart hero examples show) outsiders can have superior epistemic access to who you really are.

anchors: a lot of people in today’s world think of their true self or the answer to the question “Who are you?” as a personality hidden deep within us that only we and our closest friends have access to.
our facticity is the collection of facts that are true about us at any given moment
transcendence is our ability to change or the possibilities that we have at our disposal.
the beauty of a haiku is because we understand that we’ve given an artist total freedom within a set of limitations that we impose: five syllables, seven syllables, five syllables, go.
The primary tactic that people use in their lives to turn themselves into either pure facticity or pure transcendence like God is what Sartre calls “bad faith.”
He seems to have relegated himself to just playing the part of a waiter. He’s going through the motions trying to turn himself into pure facticity: just a waiter and nothing else.
on one hand God is perfect as he is, pure facticity. But, on the other hand, God is all-powerful and capable of bringing about any possibility he wants -- in other words, pure transcendence.
Sartre lays out his third ontological category, what he calls being-for-others.
It’s the conglomeration of all the things you’ve ever actually done in your life.
in a weird way, as outsiders, we seem to have an advantage when it comes to knowing who he really is.
